family_lesson.where_to_look_first: Start with a woody shrub, small tree, or woody vine with alternate, exstipulate leaves. Then look for resinous/aromatic tissues and small 5-part flowers. The most useful family confirmation in the local genera is a superior ovary followed by a 1-seeded drupe, often with resinous tissue in the fruit.
family_lesson.strongest_field_confirmation: Woody habit + alternate exstipulate leaves + resinous tissue + small 5-merous flowers with a nectar disk + superior ovary + drupaceous fruit.
core_characters: Trees, shrubs, or woody vines; local learner taxa are woody.
Resin canals occur in bark, petioles, major veins, flowers and/or fruit; sap may dry brown or black.
Leaves alternate in the local Rhus/Toxicodendron set and lack stipules.
Leaves may be trifoliolate or odd-pinnately compound; leaflet number and rachis form are highly useful within Rhus.
Flowers small, usually 5-merous, commonly unisexual or functionally unisexual; plants may be dioecious or otherwise sexually variable.
A nectar disk is typically present.
Ovary superior in the local teaching set, with one ovule per locule.
Fruit drupaceous and usually 1-seeded in the local genera.
Fruit surface/color and cluster position are among the best local genus-level field characters.
family_lesson.safety_note: Do not use sap contact as an identification test. Toxicodendron contains dermatitis-causing resin/urushiol; use visible morphology only.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not teach 'leaves of three = poison ivy.' Rhus aromatica also has exactly three leaflets.
Do not teach Anacardiaceae as always pinnately compound; the family includes simple and trifoliolate leaves.
Do not teach red fruit as a family character. Rhus commonly has red hairy drupes, while local poison ivy has pale whitish drupes.
Do not rely on fall color; multiple local Rhus and Toxicodendron can turn red/orange.
Do not crush unknown Anacardiaceae material to check odor/resin because Toxicodendron contact can cause dermatitis.

fastest_cues: Free-standing shrub or small tree rather than a climbing rootlet-bearing vine.
Fruit commonly red to red-orange and hairy/glandular.
Fruit/flower clusters often terminal and dense.
Leaf architecture varies strongly by species and is ideal for species-level separation.
Rhus.caution: Rhus aromatica has three leaflets and can therefore be mistaken for poison ivy if the learner stops at leaflet count.

fastest_cues: Leaves trifoliolate in the local poison-ivy complex.
Toxicodendron radicans can climb using dense adventitious/aerial rootlets or trail/scramble as a shrub.
Inflorescences and fruit clusters are axillary rather than the dense terminal pyramidal clusters typical of the local sumacs.
Drupes mature pale cream/white to grayish rather than red.
Toxicodendron.safety: All visible parts should be treated as contact hazards; do not handle for teaching demonstrations.

fast_key: Woody plant, alternate leaves, no stipules, resinous family look, drupe fruit -> consider Anacardiaceae.
Exactly 3 leaflets -> do NOT stop. Check habit and fruit.
3 leaflets + climbing/trailing stem, aerial rootlets, axillary pale/white drupes -> Toxicodendron radicans complex.
3 aromatic often lobed/coarsely toothed leaflets + low free-standing suckering shrub + red hairy drupes -> Rhus aromatica.
Many narrow leaflets + conspicuously winged rachis + deciduous tall shrub/small tree -> Rhus copallinum var. lanceolata.
5–9 thick glossy entire leaflets + evergreen/semi-evergreen large shrub -> Rhus virens.
Small odd-pinnate leaves on densely branched shrub + winged rachis + small red-orange fruit -> Rhus microphylla.

anchor_cards.look_here_first: Count many narrow leaflets, then look at the rachis itself: the tissue between leaflet pairs forms conspicuous wings.
The leaves feel visually 'evergreen': only 5–9 thick, glossy, mostly entire leaflets on a large evergreen/semi-evergreen shrub.

anchor_cards.taxonomy_note: Current POWO/FNA treatment absorbs Rhus trilobata into Rhus aromatica var. aromatica; preserve trilobata as an important older/local name but do not double-count it as a separate current species in the learner.
anchor_cards.look_here_first: Exactly three leaflets on a low free-standing suckering shrub; leaflets often lobed or coarsely toothed. Confirm with terminal red hairy fruit rather than pale poison-ivy fruit.
confirms: Early compact flower clusters often before or with leaf emergence.

anchor_cards.look_here_first: A trifoliolate woody vine, trailer, or shrub. If climbing, look for a ropey/hairy stem with dense aerial rootlets; then confirm axillary clusters of pale whitish drupes.
confirms: Terminal leaflet often on a longer petiolule; lateral leaflet bases commonly asymmetric.
Leaflet margins highly variable from nearly entire to coarsely toothed/lobed.
Pale cream/white drupes rather than red sumac fruit.
anchor_cards.safety: Do not touch or crush for ID training.
anchor_cards.local_evidence: UT Purola Preserve lists Toxicodendron radicans among naturally occurring Anacardiaceae in north Hays County; UT Travis County herbarium also lists it.

anchor_cards.taxonomy_note: Current POWO/FNA accepts Toxicodendron radicans subsp. rydbergii and treats Toxicodendron rydbergii as a synonym.
anchor_cards.look_here_first: Keep as a poison-ivy-complex comparison, not as a separate species card yet. It is generally shrubby/scrambling rather than an aggressively aerial-rooted climbing vine, but final local separation needs a dedicated review.

Sapindaceae.confusion: Alternate compound leaves and small flowers can overlap with sumacs; fruits are extremely variable.
Sapindaceae.tie_breaker: Kew notes Anacardiaceae typically has resinous sap/tissues, while Sapindaceae usually lacks sap. In local study, fruit architecture is also useful: maples have samaras, soapberry has translucent drupes, and Mexican buckeye has a capsule rather than the red hairy sumac drupe.

Rutaceae.confusion: Woody plants with compound leaves and strong odor can look similar.
Rutaceae.tie_breaker: Rutaceae has visible pellucid oil-gland dots and a citrus/rank-citrus scent but no resinous sap. Anacardiaceae lacks those pellucid gland dots and may show resin that darkens.

Rhamnaceae.confusion: Small flowers and drupaceous fruits can overlap.
Rhamnaceae.tie_breaker: Rhamnaceae usually has simple leaves with stipules present; local Rhus/Toxicodendron is exstipulate and typically compound. Rhamnaceae stamens are characteristically opposite the petals.
